t.textos.enuma-elish.pasajes.4.texto:
When Marduk heard the word of the gods,
his heart prompted him and he devised [a cunning plan].
He opened his mouth and unto Ea [he spoke],
what he had conceived in his heart he imparted [to him]:
"My blood will I take and bone [will I fashion],
I will make man, that man may […].
I will create man, who shall inhabit [the earth],
that the service of the gods may be established and [their] shrines built.
But I will alter the ways of the gods and change [their paths];
together shall they be oppressed and unto evil [they …]".
t.textos.enuma-elish.pasajes.4.fuente: Spanish version based on L. W. King, The Seven Tablets of Creation (1902), vol. I, pp. 87–89, translated here into English from the Spanish
t.textos.enuma-elish.pasajes.4.nota_acad: Here King's translation has been superseded. In line 5, dāmī is understood today as a plural, "blood", not as "my blood": "I will gather blood and bring bone into being" (dāmī luksur-ma eṣemtam lušabši), and a few lines later (VI, 31–33) it is made clear that the blood is that of Qingu, executed as the instigator of the rebellion. The created being is called lullû, "primeval man", and his function is to bear the labor of the gods so that they may rest, a theme inherited from Atrahasis. Lines 9–10 do not speak of oppressing the gods: they announce the division of the gods into two groups (Anunnaki of heaven and of the Underworld).
t.textos.enuma-elish.pasajes.4.lectura_a: Michael Tellinger (Slave Species of god, 2005), following Sitchin, reads the creation of man with divine blood as genetic engineering: the Anunnaki would have mixed their DNA with that of an earthly hominid to manufacture a slave species.

The text places the birth of man within a theological scheme of guilt and punishment (the blood of an executed rebel god) and of temple service. The mixing of clay, blood or divine saliva is a motif common to many cosmogonies and reflects the potter's craft and childbirth, not molecular biology. Population genetics and the fossil record show a continuous evolution of the genus Homo in Africa over millions of years, without any external contribution.

Current readings stress that the myth defines humanity by its labor function: humans exist so that the gods do not have to work, which reflects the economy of the great temples that lived off the labor of dependents. It is a myth that legitimizes the social order.
Synthesis of socioeconomic readings; see also Tikva Frymer-Kensky, In the Wake of the Goddesses, 1992
t.textos.gilgamesh.version: Standard Babylonian version ("He who saw the Deep"), 12 tablets, attributed to Sin-leqi-unninni (late 2nd millennium BC); copies from Ashurbanipal's library at Nineveh (7th century BC). There is an earlier Old Babylonian version ("Surpassing all other kings", c. 1800 BC) and five independent Sumerian poems about Bilgames
t.textos.gilgamesh.estructura.0.sinopsis: Prologue: praise of Gilgamesh, king of Uruk, who saw the Deep and engraved his sorrows on a stele; an invitation to walk along the walls. Gilgamesh, two-thirds god and one-third man, oppresses his city. The gods create Enkidu in the steppe; a hunter discovers him and the woman Shamhat seduces him and draws him away from the animals. Gilgamesh dreams of his coming.
t.textos.gilgamesh.estructura.1.sinopsis: Shamhat takes Enkidu to the shepherds, where he learns to eat bread and drink beer. On learning that Gilgamesh exercises a right over brides, Enkidu blocks his way; they fight and become friends. Gilgamesh proposes going to the Cedar Forest to kill Humbaba; Enkidu and the elders try to dissuade him.
t.textos.gilgamesh.estructura.2.sinopsis: Preparations for the expedition. Gilgamesh's mother, the goddess Ninsun, prays to Shamash for her son and adopts Enkidu. The elders of Uruk give advice to the travelers.
t.textos.gilgamesh.estructura.3.sinopsis: Journey to the forest: at each stage Gilgamesh asks for a dream on the mountain and has nightmares that Enkidu interprets favorably. They reach the gate of the forest and hesitate.
t.textos.gilgamesh.estructura.4.sinopsis: Entry into the Cedar Forest, dwelling of gods. Fight with Humbaba, with the help of Shamash's winds. Humbaba begs for his life; Enkidu insists on killing him and Humbaba curses them. They fell cedars and make from them a door for Enlil's temple at Nippur.
t.textos.gilgamesh.estructura.5.sinopsis: Ishtar proposes marriage to Gilgamesh, who rejects her by recalling the fate of her previous lovers. Ishtar obtains from Anu the Bull of Heaven, which devastates Uruk; the heroes kill it and Enkidu insults the goddess by throwing a leg of the bull at her.
t.textos.gilgamesh.estructura.6.sinopsis: The gods decide that Enkidu must die. Enkidu curses the cedar door, the hunter and Shamhat, and then blesses her on Shamash's advice. He dreams of the Underworld, falls ill and dies.
t.textos.gilgamesh.estructura.7.sinopsis: Gilgamesh's lament for Enkidu and the funeral: he prepares a statue and offerings for the gods of the Underworld.
t.textos.gilgamesh.estructura.8.sinopsis: Terrified by death, Gilgamesh wanders the steppe in search of Utnapishtim, the flood survivor who obtained eternal life. He passes along the path of the Sun beneath the Mashu mountains, guarded by scorpion-men, and reaches a garden of precious stones.
t.textos.gilgamesh.estructura.9.sinopsis: He meets the tavern keeper Siduri on the seashore and the boatman Urshanabi, with whom he crosses the Waters of Death. Utnapishtim answers him with a reflection on the mortal condition.
t.textos.gilgamesh.estructura.10.sinopsi: Utnapishtim tells of the flood. Gilgamesh fails the test of not sleeping for six days and seven nights. He learns of a plant of rejuvenation at the bottom of the Apsu, obtains it, and a snake steals it from him. He returns to Uruk and shows his walls to Urshanabi, closing the circle of the prologue.
t.textos.gilgamesh.estructura.11.sinopsi: An appendix translated almost word for word from a Sumerian poem (Bilgames, Enkidu and the Netherworld): Enkidu goes down to the world of the dead to recover some objects belonging to Gilgamesh, is trapped, and his spirit describes the fate of the dead.
t.textos.gilgamesh.pasajes.0.fuente: Spanish version based on R. Campbell Thompson, The Epic of Gilgamish (1928), p. 9, translated here into English from the Spanish
t.textos.gilgamesh.pasajes.0.nota_academ: Thompson translated into English hexameters, adding words in parentheses for the meter, and many of his restorations in brackets have been corrected. The first line (ša naqba īmuru) is understood today as "he who saw the Deep"; A. R. George translates: "He who saw the Deep, the country's foundation" (George, The Epic of Gilgamesh, 1999, I, 1). "The Deep" alludes at once to Ea's Apsu and to the totality of knowledge. The name of Gilgamesh, which Thompson adds with a question mark, appears with certainty in line 26 of George's edition, where there are also more lines about a cedar box holding the lapis lazuli tablet that the reader must open. The Old Babylonian version began differently: "Surpassing all other kings".
t.textos.gilgamesh.pasajes.0.lectura_act: Gilgamesh has become the emblem of humanity's "first literature". In the episode "Darmok" of Star Trek: The Next Generation, Captain Picard tells the story of Gilgamesh and Enkidu to an alien who communicates only through allusions to myths: the epic appears as a universal story of friendship.
Star Trek: The Next Generation, "Darmok", season 5, 1991
t.textos.gilgamesh.pasajes.1.ref: Tablet I, col. II (Thompson's lines 1 and 29–41)
t.textos.gilgamesh.pasajes.1.texto:
Two-thirds of him are divine, and [one-third of him human] […]
[…]
(And so), at (the cry of) their laments, [Anu] gave ear, he called the lady Aruru:
"It was you, O Aruru, who made [(the first seed of) mankind (?)]: now make his companion,
that he may [meet Gilgamesh], yes, on the day of his pleasure,
that they may fight with each other and he may give [rest] to Uruk".
When the goddess Aruru heard this, in her mind she conceived
(at once this) design of Anu and, washing her hands, (then) Aruru
pinched off some clay, in the steppe she shaped it: [(thus) in the steppe]
she made Enkidu, a warrior, (as though) born (and) begotten,
(yes), a double of Ninurta, [and she covered] his whole body
with hair; like a woman he gathered his locks in a band;
his hair sprang up luxuriant like (the beards of) barley.
He knew neither people nor land; he was clad like Sumuqan.
Even with the gazelles he grazed on the grass, together with the cattle
he drank his fill; with the beasts his heart delighted in the water.
t.textos.gilgamesh.pasajes.1.fuente: Spanish version based on R. Campbell Thompson, The Epic of Gilgamish (1928), pp. 9–11, translated here into English from the Spanish
t.textos.gilgamesh.pasajes.1.nota_academ: "Two-thirds god, one-third man" is theological arithmetic: his mother is the goddess Ninsun and his father the deified king Lugalbanda; some texts about the creation of Gilgamesh by Belet-ili explain the division. The gesture of Aruru (a mother goddess) is read today as "she pinched off clay and threw it into the steppe", an act of pottery and of birth. George translates Enkidu's epithet as "offspring of silence, knit strong by Ninurta". Sumuqan (Shakkan) is the god of wild animals: Enkidu goes naked or clad like the beasts. The passage establishes the opposition between steppe and city that runs through the work.
t.textos.gilgamesh.pasajes.1.lectura_ast: Sitchin and, on television, Giorgio Tsoukalos (Ancient Aliens) present "two-thirds god" as proof of a genetic hybrid between Anunnaki and humans, and the creation of Enkidu as another biological manipulation.

The formula belongs to Mesopotamian royal ideology, in which kings present themselves as sons or protégés of gods; the proportions make no genetic sense (a direct descendant of a goddess and a man would be "half and half"), and the scribes themselves debated how they fitted together. Enkidu is modeled in clay, like the first man in other myths, to embody the wild man who preceded civilization.
t.textos.gilgamesh.pasajes.2.ref: Tablet II (Thompson), cols. II–III = Old Babylonian Pennsylvania version, cols. ii–iii
t.textos.gilgamesh.pasajes.2.texto:
While Gilgamesh (thus) reveals his dream, Enkidu sits before the hetaera […]
(And so) Enkidu took his pleasure six days and seven nights with the courtesan in their union.
Then the nymph broke into speech and (thus) said to Enkidu:
"(Yes, when) I look at you, (even) like a god, O Enkidu, you shall be;
why with the beasts (of the field) do you (always) roam the steppe?
Up, for I will take you to [Uruk], of the broad markets, (yes), to the Holy Temple, the dwelling of Anu.
O Enkidu, come, let me guide you to Eanna, the dwelling of Anu, where [Gilgamesh] (lives),
(he), the supreme of creation; and you, yes, you [will embrace him]
like [a woman], and (even) [like] yourself [you will love him]".
[…]
He (before) had been used to sucking the milk of wild beasts.
The bread that she set before him he broke, but he looked and was dumbfounded:
Enkidu did not know how to eat bread, nor had he knowledge of how to drink the beer.
(Then) the woman answered, speaking to Enkidu:
"Enkidu, taste the bread, (for) it is the essence of life;
drink the beer as well, it is the custom of the land".
Enkidu ate of the bread until he was sated,
he drank seven cups of beer; his spirit rose and, exultant,
glad was his heart and radiant his face […];
with oil he anointed the hair of his body, and (so) he became human.
t.textos.gilgamesh.pasajes.2.fuente: Spanish version based on R. Campbell Thompson, The Epic of Gilgamish (1928), pp. 16–17, translated here into English from the Spanish
t.textos.gilgamesh.pasajes.2.nota_academ: Here Thompson incorporates the Old Babylonian tablet from Pennsylvania (c. 1800 BC), not the standard version. He translates the term ḫarimtu as "hetaera" or "courtesan"; the woman's name is Shamhat ("the voluptuous one"). The meaning of ḫarimtu is debated: it does not always designate a prostitute, and J. Assante (1998) proposed "unmarried woman outside male authority". Thompson translates "mead": it is in fact beer (šikaru). Eating bread, drinking beer, anointing oneself and getting dressed are the features that define civilization in Mesopotamia. The comparison "like a woman you will love him" reappears in Gilgamesh's dreams.
t.textos.gilgamesh.pasajes.2.lectura_act: Susan Ackerman analyzes the vocabulary of love between Gilgamesh and Enkidu ("like a woman"), together with the dreams and the lament of Tablet VIII, and compares it with David and Jonathan. She concludes that the text deliberately plays with the erotic without fitting into modern categories of homosexuality.
Susan Ackerman, When Heroes Love: The Ambiguity of Eros in the Stories of Gilgamesh and David, 2005
